problem: The arithmetic gives a 1,558-byte Ethernet frame for a 1,500-byte application message. Standard Ethernet MTU is 1,500 bytes of IP payload, so 1,500 bytes of application data plus 20-byte TCP and 20-byte IP headers is 1,540 bytes and cannot fit in one Ethernet frame; max Ethernet frame size is 1,518 bytes. In practice TCP MSS limits application data to 1,460 bytes or IP fragments the packet.
fix: Use a 1,460-byte application message: overhead is still 58 bytes, frame is 1,518 bytes, efficiency is 1,460 ÷ 1,518 = 96.2%. Or state explicitly that the calculation ignores Ethernet MTU and fragmentation.

problem: The statement that 'every layer adds its own header' is not true for the physical layer. The physical layer sends the frame as bits/signals and adds no header, so a student may wrongly think physical-layer encapsulation exists.
fix: Say the transport, network and data-link layers add headers (data link also adds a trailer); the physical layer sends the resulting frame as signals without adding a header.
